However, while the prospect of obtaining high‐frequency, high‐quality, low‐cost data is appealing, determining the right UAV platform, sensors, and data processing pipelines can create a high barrier to entry for many interested researchers (Harris et al. 2019). Modern programs and algorithms create opportunities to process UAV data into unique products, and new types of information can be pulled out of flight recordings through object‐ and pixel‐based classification approaches. However, the development of meaningful, reproducible, and useful products is still an evolving field (Woodget et al. 2017). Here, we demonstrate how a UAV approach can be used to estimate the length of a gillnet in operation (Figure 6). Despite the realization of basic data (i.e., net length in meters), it is possible to estimate the swept area occupied by the fishing gear in the water. Based on the evolution of processing methods and future possibilities, post‐collection data can be integrated into other frameworks or processed into brand new datasets.

Manned aircraft are often deemed efficient for sampling large areas, and arguably provide the greatest area sampled per unit cost (Watts et al. 2012). To sample an equivalent area with the currently available UAV technology and regulations, many separate flights would likely be required, demanding either much longer sampling windows or multiple pilots and UAVs (Colefax et al. 2019). However, this does not detract from the many interesting questions in SSF studies at smaller spatial scales that can be answered with this approach (e.g., number of fishing boats deployed in a given area or number of stationary fishing gears).

In recent years, a great deal of effort has been invested in the development of analytical approaches to systematically describe and quantify movements on water surfaces such as swimming dynamics, collective behavior, and interactions of surface‐oriented marine species (Rieucau et al. 2018). This approach can be used to analyze analogous patterns produced by fisheries, such as the displacement of fishing boats and their fishing operations (Figure 2B), the tidal and/or wind‐oriented movements of fishing gear (Figures 3A, 3B), and size estimates of gill nets (Figure S4A) and/or cast nets (Figure S4B) measured in pixels. These data processing options demonstrate how

based on surface‐oriented processes without having to rely on time‐consuming post‐processing procedures. However, such “static” approaches to the analysis of images from UAV surveys should be used in combination with automated video post processing to accurately depict the displacement dynamics of target fisheries. An ongoing challenge for the development of UAV video analysis is related to the capability of the system to estimate and subtract the movement of the UAV in relation to that of the target boat when trawling, for example. As a possible way to correct for this difference, Rieucau et al. (2018) proposed considering UAV motion as discrete image displacements, which would permit the establishment of reference points for the isolation of one or more moving objects before omitting background movement. Even so, the development of these approaches for fishery research would represent a complementary next step in the process after the basic applications discussed in this paper.

Given the limited understanding of the undesirable impacts caused by low‐altitude UAV flights, we must strive to reduce the risk of disruption, report positive and negative observational responses (i.e., from researchers and managers who are currently using UAV tools), and develop criteria for best practices in field research (Hodgson and Koh 2016). The development of best practices and standardization of techniques will ensure the comparability of data among different fishing zones, regions, and countries.
